turns.text: Sir, field report number four, and the last, on the electricity file. Today: where electricity is going. In the last reports I told you the grid's biggest problem: power can't be stored. What's made must be used in the same second. And that is changing right before my eyes. Warehouse-sized batteries, sunlight that became some of their cheapest power, and a country that built half its grid on its roofs. And at the end, a number command must know: who here still has no light bulb at all.

turns.text: Start with the original problem: power can't be stored. But that's starting to change. The old way: water. When power is spare and cheap, they pump water up to a lake on a mountain. When they need it, they let it fall through a turbine. A battery.. made of water. The new way: batteries like the one in your phone, but the size of warehouses. In twenty twenty-five alone, a hundred and twelve gigawatts of them went in on the planet. And for the first time they passed water. The reason: price. Storing a kilowatt-hour cost about fifteen hundred dollars in twenty ten. By twenty twenty-five, a hundred and eight. Down more than ninety percent. The one thing here that gets cheaper.

turns.text: So how does a battery store anything? The one in your phone, your car, the warehouse: nearly the same idea. Inside are two sides, with a wall between them. And tiny atoms of a metal called lithium move from one side to the other. When you charge, the power pushes the lithium to one side, like sending people up a ladder. When you use the phone, the lithium goes back, and the electrons that came with it have to go round the outside, through the wire, running the device on the way. So a battery isn't a box of electricity, sir. It's a ladder, with lithium climbing up and down. Every trip wears the ladder a little. That's why a phone battery after a few years doesn't last like it did. It isn't tired. It's old.

turns.text: Its most famous story was a bet. In twenty seventeen, a state in Australia kept losing power. The owner of an electric car company posted online: I'll build you the world's biggest battery in a hundred days.. or it's free. It was done in about sixty-three. In its first year it saved the grid about forty million Australian dollars. Because a battery answers any wobble in the balance in under a second. A normal plant needs minutes. First time I've seen a rich human bet.. and the people win.

turns.text: The other game changer: the sun. Solar power got about ninety percent cheaper since twenty ten. It's now some of the cheapest power they've ever built. One problem. Here's demand through the day. The sun peaks at noon. So what's left for other plants is very low at noon.. then shoots up like a wall at sunset, when the sun leaves and people get home. Engineers call this shape the duck curve. Look at it. It really is a duck. Here batteries come in: they charge at noon from the spare sun, and empty after sunset. They move noon into the night. Wind is the same story: it comes when it feels like it, not when demand does. Together the two made about seventeen percent of the planet's power in twenty twenty-five. And without storage, some countries have so much power at noon that the price drops below zero. They pay you to use it. Yes, sir. This planet now pays to get rid of electricity.

turns.text: Summary of the whole file, sir. One: electricity is charges moving round a circuit, as direct or alternating current. Two: it's made by a spinning magnet, travels at high voltage, and the grid is a balance set every second. Three: if the balance breaks, it falls like dominoes. And four: batteries and the sun are changing the rules now. But hundreds of millions still have no bulb, and that problem was never the physics. The electricity file is closed. Four reports.
